pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: How does Go decide that `*CountingWriter` satisfies `io.Writer`, given that your code never says so? What does this buy you compared to languages with an `implements` keyword?
expected_points: satisfaction is structural: the compiler checks the method set against the interface, no declaration needed
a type can satisfy interfaces written after it, by authors who never saw it
implementing packages don't import the interface's package, so dependencies stay pointed at the consumer and coordination/import cycles disappear

questions.prompt: `Write` on `CountingWriter` has a pointer receiver. Why does `io.Copy(w, src)` fail to compile while `io.Copy(&w, src)` works?
expected_points: the method set of CountingWriter (the value) excludes pointer-receiver methods, so the value does not satisfy io.Writer
the method set of *CountingWriter includes both value- and pointer-receiver methods
the interface stores a copy; calling a pointer method on that copy would mutate an unreachable value, so the rule blocks it at compile time

questions.prompt: The starter's `Write` returned `(0, nil)` and `io.Copy` failed with `io.ErrShortWrite`. What does the `io.Writer` contract require of `Write`'s return values, and what else does it forbid?
expected_points: Write must report how many bytes of p it consumed, with a non-nil error whenever that is less than len(p)
(0, nil) after receiving bytes claims nothing was consumed with no error, which io.Copy correctly treats as a short write
Write must not modify or retain p — the caller still owns the slice

questions.prompt: `Saver` is defined in the `report` package, next to `Archive`, and has exactly one method. Defend both choices against a teammate who wants a ten-method `Storage` interface exported by the storage package.
expected_points: the consumer defines the minimal behavior it needs, so the interface documents Archive's true requirements
providers stay concrete and satisfy it implicitly without importing report
small interfaces are satisfied by more types and make test fakes trivial — the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction

questions.prompt: `io.Copy` moved data from a `strings.Reader` through your `UpperWriter` into a `bytes.Buffer` — three types that know nothing about each other. What makes that composition possible, and why does so much of the stdlib funnel through `io.Reader`/`io.Writer`?
expected_points: each piece depends only on the one-method interfaces, not on concrete types
any Reader source composes with any Writer sink, so n types give n interoperable pieces instead of n-squared adapters
tiny interfaces are the stdlib's common currency, which is why wrapping writers like UpperWriter slot in anywhere

questions.prompt: `NewUpperWriter` accepts an `io.Writer` but returns `*UpperWriter`, not `io.Writer`. Why is 'accept interfaces, return structs' the idiomatic shape?
expected_points: accepting an interface makes the function usable with any conforming destination
returning the concrete type keeps the full method set available to callers
callers can always narrow a concrete type to their own interface later; a returned interface hides methods and abstracts prematurely
